utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning -- good afternoon, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Oric. Can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honour, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in my mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Oric and good afternoon to you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, also good afternoon to the Defence. I'm here together with co-counsel Ms. Patricia Sellers and our case manager Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour, my name is Vasvija Vidovic and together with Mr. John Jones I appear with Mr. Naser Oric. With us is our legal assistants Mr. Mehic and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic and good afternoon to you and your team. Any preliminaries? Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, two issues, first related to the scheduling of witnesses and the second to the 98 bis scheduling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: First, witness scheduling. Last week --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, let me find my own documents on that, please. Yes. Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, last week, we could confirm to Your Honours that we should be able to finalise the -- our case on the Tuesday, the 31st of May. After that, we learnt that two days were not available for court, meaning the 19th and the 20th of May, and we accept to reschedule the witness concerned. Well, we are today filing, project to file, a new witness list to the parties later on in the day, I think after the break. And currently, it is the Prosecution intention to finalise its case by the 2nd of June, meaning two days in addition to those earlier-mentioned days. With a view to this re-scheduling of witnesses, with no guarantee of course that witnesses can, in fact, attend on the days we want them to. There is a degree of uncertainty regarding expected testimony days. However, we don't expect that to be a significant problem. This means also that Prosecution suggests to the Trial Chamber to take into consideration scheduling of the start of the 98 bis submission, whenever we add two days to our additional planning, but in addition, I would raise on my initiative the issue as such of the scheduling of the 98 bis submission. Prosecution has given further thought to the time interval between the Defence 98 bis submission and the response by the Prosecution, and thus time required for the Prosecution to formulate a response. And that time was, as allowed by Trial Chamber, three days plus a weekend, in total five days. As per instructions, I submit now the Prosecution should be able to cut down the time required to respond. We want to shorten the procedure as much as possible, with each side having as limited time of preparation as allowed by Trial Chamber to prepare, and in that field, we should be able to prepare in one day, one working day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That would be extremely fine with us. I am going to not even give you the floor for the time being, Mr. Jones or Ms. Vidovic, because I am informed you have a problem in that you need to be in the United Kingdom for professional purposes that came up unexpectedly and on which you don't have control and which are essential for your career.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will of course accommodate you, we will do our best to accommodate you, as much as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. If I might just say I'm sorry to burden the Court with that. I've always tried to avoid any professional commitments elsewhere having any conflict with this trial. It's simply that I sit part-time as an immigration judge in the U.K. and there is a compulsory training for all judges which if I missed that I would lose my status as a judge. And so it's just to request that the 6th and 7th of June could be avoided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can rest assured, Mr. Jones, that we are fully aware that you've been - not only you but also Ms. Vidovic - have been cooperating with this Tribunal. And on matters like this you will certainly find the cooperation of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, I'm very much obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So -- now, let's -- we'll work this out. I wouldn't like to take much time of the sitting, as much as possible, so that you give -- if necessary we will work out a different timetable in chambers when we are not sitting. But more or less, the indication is as follows. Then we will go back to what we said we would expect in the first place, namely that frankly speaking, the moment you finish with your last witness, okay, here it's a little bit different, but the day after, supposedly, we would say, now, we would like to hear submissions. Mr. Jones will stand up and make a half an hour intervention, sometimes it's even less than that, or maybe one hour at the most. And you will be expected to stand up and respond and in other words we should finish that within easy within one sitting. So we'll give you a little bit more than one hour, of course, but let's take it up in my chambers at some later point in time. But in the meantime you can put your mind at rest that you will be able to attend this training, judicial training, in the United Kingdom. There will be absolutely no spokes in the wheel from our side for sure. And that -- we appreciate also your coming forward and showing your availability to lessen the -- that. Then we need to discuss, because this impinges a little bit on whether we should give our decision. I think more or less there will be either -- two alternative roads to follow. One would be to hand down the decision as we had suggested earlier, that is after the commitment that we have with you. But that was because we would have finished the whole 92 bis process of submissions a couple of days before. So it would have made sense. Now it wouldn't probably make sense on our part to sleep on the decision, Rule 98 bis decision, for that long. And we'll probably -- I mean we need to discuss amongst ourselves, obviously. But we will probably come down with the decision earlier, unless we find out that there are some issues which necessarily has to be postponed. Which may not be the case. But we will discuss amongst ourselves and we will have a short meeting with you in camera either tomorrow or early next week. And that will be the position. In other words, if we finish on the 2nd with the testimony - and I don't see why, to be honest with you, the last two -- the witnesses for the 26th and 27th of May, and the 36 and 38th and 31st of May, maybe I don't know enough, but I frankly feel that they could be reduced to one day each, both sides. This is a chain of custody, two of the chain of custody witnesses. And I honestly think that you can easily split the time, one and a half hours each, and cover these two witnesses. That's my opinion. But we will discuss that when we will have the meeting in my Chamber next week. All right? Early next week. In the meantime, please do check whether you can really reschedule those two witnesses to testify witnesses to testify less, for less than three hours each for the Prosecution, because I honestly don't think that testifying on the chain of custody requires three hours on your side. I mean, I don't know. I may be wrong because obviously you know more than I do about these two witnesses but -- actually I know nothing about these two witnesses. So that's the message and we will talk about it in my Chamber and then we will report back in open session. The idea is not to take much of today's time. Yes, I saw you, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have certain preliminary issues to raise with respect to this witness who is about to testify. In respect of this witness, if I may, Your Honour, in respect of this witness, we have received a statement, a very brief one, and a very generalised one, given to the investigators of the Tribunal. Yesterday, at around 7.30, we received the proofing notes with a list of exhibits containing 36 documents. Many of these documents were documents we had heard of for the first time. We tried to establish in every possible way what documents these were, in order to prepare for the cross-examination today. This morning, when we applied to the Prosecutor asking for copies of the documents to be delivered to us, they said that we had received them and the receipt was number 51, relating to the Cobblestone documents, and the second solution was to find the documents on the EDS. First of all, I have here Receipt 51, and of course we have not received these documents. I know very well which documents we received. We did not receive a single one of these documents. And I think it is not good enough for us to be told to look in EDS and Cobblestone a day before the testimony of the witness. We, however, did our best to find the documents. We worked on it all morning but we were unable to find these documents on EDS. I'm referring to six documents now, and when we requested to have copies of the documents delivered to us, we received them at 12.42 in our locker. These are documents which require analysis, and I wish to say that the Prosecutors knew a long time ago that we would be sitting in the afternoon today and tomorrow morning. So this is really unfair. We are being put in a situation in which we are unable to prepare properly for the cross-examination. In addition to witness, in the witness list, they mention P209, saying this was an order signed by Hamid Salihovic. However, P210 -- I apologise to the interpreters. They mention document P210, signed by Hamid Salihovic. However, the document under this number has nothing to do with Hamid Salihovic. They are really putting us in a situation in which we cannot prepare properly for the cross-examination. In addition to this, ten minutes before the start of the hearing, they told us they would not be using 11 of these documents. Your Honours, I'm really doing my best to be cooperative, as is my team. But every time we find ourselves in a situation in which we do not know what documents the Prosecutor is planning to tender and use, or they send us lists of documents which they do not use at all. They shorten the list and so on and so forth. I believe, Your Honours, that a long time ago you issued a decision whereby we have to receive the lists within a reasonable time limit before the hearing so that we can prepare properly. The situation, however, is getting worse. And -- as this part of the trial is nearing its close, the situation is getting worse. The Prosecutor planned three hours for this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three hours. I will, Your Honour. I think that I should not abbreviate my cross-examination, and it will not be less than three hours. Therefore, I ask Your Honours to impose a time limit on the Prosecutor or I cannot guarantee that I will be able to conclude my cross-examination tomorrow. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have anything to state on what has been mentioned by Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unfortunately we are not in a position to comment ourselves because we don't receive the proofing notes to start with, and the only list of documents that I have is what my secretary received yesterday and I don't know whether this is the list that you are referring to or whether you have an updated one. So please, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you for this opportunity. In terms of learned counsel, the proofing notes were sent last night immediately after the witness had been proofed, and among the first things that was written in the proofing note is that the witness would be spoken to again this morning and if there were any changes, those notes would certainly be conveyed to you. I think that we have done that. In terms of the document list, this witness was scheduled to testify for one day. I will endeavour to keep the Prosecution case down to one day, although now we are almost a half hour into the session. The reason that there were documents deleted in many ways was keeping this in mind. If Your Honours would just permit me one minute. There was a mistake made in one of the original documents, and that was document P495. That was discovered after we sent it to you last night and I understand that the case manager then forwarded you immediately notice of our error to say, right, we do not want P95 [sic] -- as a matter of fact it's Prosecution Exhibit 496. In reviewing the list of documents last night myself, working here until after 11 o'clock and with the witness this morning, the effort was made to ensure this witness's testimony would take no longer than one court day. As a result of trying to shorten his testimony but making sure his testimony remained relevant, reviewed the list of exhibits because we thought it would be much worse to include new exhibits today rather than to take exhibits away. Now, there were ten exhibits that were removed from the list and they were, as a matter of fact, Defence exhibits, 205 through 215 that, upon using them in a proofing session today, I said that they might not be as necessary. Not that they aren't relevant documents but this would be one way in which we might be able to minimise the Court time. There were a couple of other documents that on second thought this morning documents that are familiar, documents that are basically decrees of law that we decided we can have the witness speak about and not necessarily again present them. So in that sense, yes, the Defence is right; the exhibit list that is changed. It has been minimised. I believe it's going to make a more efficient court session. In terms of the documents that are no -- that are not either Prosecution or Defence Exhibit documents, those are documents that came from a collection that we ourselves do not have the translation for until 12.00 this afternoon. They are documents that we will certainly use, but I would like to say that they are one-page documents that pertain to, as this Court will see, very brief correspondence. Now, our impression was that in order for the Defence to have access, or look at these documents as quick as possible, they be placed in a locker or you could just pull them electronically of the system. That's part of our policy of our office, is the electronic disclosure system it used for some of the purposes. But they were placed in the locker so they wouldn't have to fish during the night. And we have e-mail traffic that did state as much. Your Honours, I would just say that what we have tried to do with a witness who could easily go over a couple of days for the Prosecution case is to maintain what we offered in to the Trial Chamber that we would try it in one day. As a result of that, we've tried to amend the exhibit list and to notify Defence counsel not only as soon as possible but immediately. And I understand with where Defence counsel says they might require more time to prepare. The Prosecution certainly doesn't object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- but let it be known for the record that this was done having the Trial Chamber's interest in mind as well as the Defence interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you both. Let's try and be practical about it. I understand that being able or put in a position which you can defend your client properly is a right and not a privilege. It's a right. As we go along, if you encounter problems and you think that you are not in a position to defend your client because of these documents or small number of them, please let me -- let us know and we will try and find a remedy. For the future, please try to avoid as much as possible this recurring because not only it has cost us almost half an hour, but it creates difficulties in general. Usher, could you please bring the witness in. You need to finish today. Ms. Sellers, maximum you will not get more than 15 minutes tomorrow maximum, if you don't finish today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm cognizant of that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder if you said 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I said 15. The transcripts are anti-Defence. It's 15, 1-5 minutes. Because you will get 15 and you will get the rest. And the understanding is that you will try and leave us that five to ten minutes in case we need to put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Judge Hogic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Enver Hogic. Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. My name is Carmel Agius. I am the Presiding Judge and I come from the Island of Malta. To my right I have Judge Hans Hendrik Brydensholt from the Kingdom of Denmark. To my left, I have Judge Alban Eser who comes from Germany. Together, we form the Trial Chamber in this case which has been instituted against Naser Oric. Welcome once more. As you see, I'm speaking in English, and there will be questions put to you in the English language, at least from the Prosecution side, and everything will be interpreted to you in your own language. If at any time there are problems with the interpretation that you are receiving, or if the sound level is not to your liking, please draw our attention straightaway and we will find a remedy to that. You're soon going to start giving evidence as a Prosecution witness. Our rules require that before you do so, you make a solemn declaration which is contained in the piece of paper that Madam Usher is handing to you now. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Judge. Please make yourself comfortable. Madam Patricia Sellers, whom you've met already, will go first. She will be examining you in chief. And then we'll have the cross-examination tomorrow. Madam Vidovic, who is lead counsel for Mr. Oric will cross-examine you tomorrow and then hopefully we try and do our best to finish with your testimony tomorrow so that you can go back home. And to your work as well. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hogic. Just for purposes of the record would you state again your full name to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: My name is Enver Hogic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, might I ask you: Is your ethnicity that of Bosnian, Muslim Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: I'm a Bosniak by nationality, and a Muslim by religion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would ask the Trial Chamber, might I try and lead him in some of the background information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Lease please go ahead. I would expect you to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, are you a graduate of the University of Sarajevo law school?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I graduated in 1977.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And in 1979 did you take training from the JNA specialising in communications?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: That was in 1979, during my military service in Belgrade and Kumanova.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And in 1992, is it true that you volunteered and you joined the army of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 10th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And later on, a couple months later, were you mobilised under the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina after it become an independent state?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: It was in the month of July that I joined the Territorial Defence district staff in Tuzla. I wouldn't say that I was mobilised. Rather I volunteered. I saw this as a patriotic duty that I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And where did you work first when you went to the territorial staff office in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: That was the first place where I was involved. The information centre, with the Tuzla municipality. There I discharged duties that I had from before as a military conscript in the former Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. I worked as a communications officer, a signals officer. I was setting up radio and telephone lines for the purposes of what was then the War Presidency of Tuzla municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And in July 1992, did you become the deputy chief of the legal services at headquarters in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was with the district staff in Tuzla, which had already been established. I became deputy chief of the legal services. The chief was Mr. Meho Nusic [as interpreted], and I was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And what department did the legal services come under at the district headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: It was part -- part of the staff, of the district staff of the TO. It was a legal service which was part of the sector for moral guidance which was a higher level organisational unit within the staff itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And in December of 1992, did you become chief of the legal services?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I replaced Mr. Nusret Mesic who went to a different job with the Defence Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And in April of 1993, wasn't the legal services upgraded to a department, a legal department, and you remained the chief of that service?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: In April 1993, legal service, which had been part of the sector for moral guidance up to that point, became an independent sector. And as such, pursuant to an order by the B and H General Staff, BH army General Staff, it became a sector headed by the commander of the 2nd Corps. That was me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would you tell the Trial Chamber, then, what was your rank within the army during the time period that you were the commander?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: At the time, I did not have a formal rank, but there were establishment posts, so-called establishment posts, and for each of these establishment posts, whoever was the incumbent had the rank either of a colonel or of a brigadier. And it was later on, in 1994, as the army structure evolved that I was granted the rank of a Captain 1st Class. One day before I left the army in 1996, I was made a major.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, as the assistant commander for legal matters, did you give legal advice to the corps commanders, the commanders of 2 Corps?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: I understand -- I'm not sure the interpretation is ideal. I was the assistant commander for legal matters, not deputy commander. So may that be amended, please. On the other hand, in that position, I was always in a situation whenever required to give my commander, regardless of who it was, proper legal advice or instructions on how they should act in a given situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Trial Chamber the names of the corps commanders that you served under between 1992 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: The first corps commander was Mr. Zeljko Knez. Before him -- before that, Zeljko Knez was a former JNA officer who switched sides and joined the BH army. First, he was the commander of the district staff of the Territorial Defence and the structure of the units was the same as those in the army. He was appointed the first commander of the 2nd Corps of the BH army. He was followed by his erstwhile deputy, Mr. Hasim Saric [as interpreted], who remained in that position, unless I'm mistaken, between March 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Finish what you are saying and then I need to ask you something to clarify something. You were saying, "He was followed by his erstwhile deputy Mr. Hasim Saric who remained in that position, unless I'm mistaken." This is precisely what I wanted to ask you. Is it Saric or Sadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "S" in the Bosnian language means "sh", Sadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not Saric, because in the transcript it came out as Saric. Okay, yes, Judge. You may proceed. Sorry for having interrupted you like this but -- so he was followed by Mr. Sadic between March 1993, if you were not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He remained in that position until as late as October 1994 when he became Bosnia's military attache in Turkey. He was succeeded by Mr. Sead Delic who remained in that position until the end of the war and for a while after.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, as part of your duties as the assistant commander for legal matters, did you give advice to the corps commanders on the treatment of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you give advice to the corps commanders from 2 Corps on the legalities of waging armed conflict or war or battles and operations therein?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you also give legal advice to the 2 Corps commanders on what could be considered criminal acts committed by members of the army?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. In that respect, the commander would use his authority as corps commander to issue binding orders to subordinate units within the corps. These were no mere oral instructions. They were more. The commander would receive proposals from his assistants, including myself, and turn these into orders that he would then pass on to subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, could you briefly tell the Trial Chamber whether the Geneva Conventions were part of the basis of a legal advice or apparatus that you used in your position as assistant commander for legal matters.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That much is certain. The reason is simple. Whenever combat operations were being carried out, especially those of an offensive nature, those carried out by the corps in 1992 and 1993, all of the subordinate units were admonished that they should act with due care, and in full compliance with the Geneva Conventions. If I may try to clarify, by the Chamber's leave. Throughout the war we worked closely with the International Red Cross, especially as regards one particular area, namely the rights enshrined in the Geneva Conventions. It was along these lines that we got in touch with the Red Cross mission in Tuzla where it was based throughout the war and requested from them printed material that we distributed throughout the units within the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps. We used these to spread knowledge and to teach our troops on how they should treat the enemy as well as any civilians that might happen to be within their area of responsibility. How to treat prisoners, how to treat wounded prisoners, and also to teach them about all other matters that might have been relevant at the time. I'm not sure I can remember all of them right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown Prosecution Exhibit 272.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please look -- in the English version it's page number 2, and the title would be, "Order on the Application of the Rules of the International Law of the War in the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, are you familiar with this order and did you use it in carrying out your duties as the assistant commander for legal matters?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Even before it was published in this form, in the Official Gazette of the BH army, it had been published already in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as something that had been adopted by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And this is something that we were familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And can I ask you that in the supervision -- or I'm sorry. In the advice that you would give, the legal advice to the corps commanders and to other members of the Bosnian army, would you inform them that they were bound by the customs of war that were recognised under international law as set forth in Article 1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection. I have not yet heard the witness say that he advised anyone else in the army. He was talking about advising corps commanders or, rather, the commanders of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's what -- why I asked Ms. Vidovic to intervene before the witness gave his answer because I would have had exactly the same objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour he testified about training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to have the witness explain this chain of getting the troops according to him informed of their responsibilities under the Geneva Conventions, how it operated. In other words, who had the responsibility and who was informing or making the troops aware of these responsibilities because it was certainly not him. So he needs to tell us what his personal role was in this chain of imparting information to the troops, and where it was taken up by others after he had left or done what was within his responsibility. I think we need to explain that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, certainly I will do that. And I just wanted to respond that I thought that he had indicated that there was information imparted to other than the corps commanders. But let's go to Your Honour's question you've heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please explain how the advice was imparted to other members, how the chain worked in terms of information to other members of the 2nd Corps, and not just the corps commanders, in terms of the rules and regulations, particularly those pertaining to international law.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is -- is there a problem of interpretation? If it's so, interpretation, yes. Otherwise let him answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go ahead with your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a member of the command of the 2nd Corps. The job of the members of the command did not end once you left the building or the actual establishment of the corps command. Whenever necessary, whenever the commander saw fit, he would set up various teams of a varying composition. I myself was involved with some of these teams or groups, whatever you like to call them. These groups or teams went to certain units which had a level of an operations group or a brigade that was within an operations group. The objective was to maintain discipline or to take such measures as were required in a certain unit. Meetings were organised jointly with the commanders of these units and these meetings were used to point out which steps should be taken in a given situation. Among other things, we used these meetings to explain about the application of the international -- of international law. And the international law of war. Within the corps, and the units that were within its composition, we also organised working meetings to give advice for all units and the heads of all units, from battalion and brigade level and down the chain of command, and their assistants. And we advised them on how international law should be applied and the international law of war as well. We also consulted with the International Red Cross that was based in Tuzla at the time. I'm not sure if that answers your question. If there is any further clarification that needs providing, please remind me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make sure is that basically, you are in a position to confirm to us that this ultimately reached the troops that would be engaged in combat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This information on the application of the international law of war would be given to the commanders and it was their duty to pass this information on to the combatants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My question is precisely: Are you in a position to confirm that it wasn't just the duty of the commanders to pass this information on to the troops, but that they did actually pass on this information to the troops? That the troops, in other words, were indeed kept fully aware of their responsibilities under international criminal law and under international law, anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my might I just say one technical matter we are looking at page 2 of the English and I believe that on the ELMO we have page 1 up. Could I ask the usher --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wasn't check being the ELMO, Ms. Sellers. Yes, it is definitely page 1, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would just like to ask Mr. Hogic then would he look at number 3 on the order.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And does this confirm what you say that in order to become acquainted with the rules of international law, we'd organise regular training in the armed forces to which members of the armed forces shall be subject? Does that confirm the type of information dissemination and training that the legal department performed?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We might take that exhibit back from the witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Usher, please. Thank you, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, in continuing to discuss the legal basis, or the applicable rules and regulations that 2 Corps and possibly the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina followed, I'd like to ask you were there any criminal codes incorporated or used in terms of the law that was applicable to the army and particularly members of the army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I will allow the objection now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not comfortable with my learned friend referring to 2 Corps and possibly the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think we need to be clear. I've understood so far any references to troops is solely to the members of the 2nd Corps and I think we need to be clear. Is she asking about the army generally or the 2nd Corps or the 3rd Corps or the 1st Corps? We can't be vague in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree with him. It's easy to specify.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I agree with my learned friend, but I think the document we have just seen comes from someone who certainly had power over more than just 2 Corps, the order that comes from Mr. Izetbegovic. And after the witness has agreed that yes, that was applicable law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer the question for the witness. So -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour might the witness answer the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer the question for the witness. The witness has heard the exchange of between you, Mr. Jones and myself. Actually. And I think he knows exactly how to answer this question. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic would you please answer the question, then.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: If you could just please remind me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right. The question was, then: Were there any criminal codes also incorporated into the rules or regulations that were applicable to 2 Corps and possibly to the Bosnian army in general?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: After Bosnia and Herzegovina declared its independence, certain regulations were passed that were adopted from the system of the former Yugoslavia pursuant to a decision by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a binding, legal act. And this was then applied as the regulations of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Among other regulations that were adopted, the Criminal Code of the SFRY was adopted as far as its general provisions, and also its part that referred to crimes against the army, the part that pertained to war, and the part that refers to the Geneva Conventions. We need to be absolutely clear on this. These are regulations of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These are no military regulations. These are regulations that were passed or adopted by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the strength of its authority. According to the constitution, it still had the right to stand in for the assembly or for the parliament, if you like. That's why there were these binding, legal orders that once passed in the parliament became laws. This --this was the case with the Criminal Code too, both as concerned its general and special provisions. All these provisions were applied throughout the war until the new criminal codes -- new criminal codes were adopted once the war was over and once there was no longer any imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now were these criminal codes applied to the armed forces under the 2nd Corps as well as the members of the armed forces within the larger army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: The code has a general nature. It applies to all those whom it concerns. It is used to prosecute illegal behaviour. Members of the 2nd Corps as well - as all the other members of the BH army and this applied throughout the war - as soon as anyone committed a crime, this person would have been prosecuted by the relevant bodies, the bodies whose job it was to prosecute any such individuals. Regardless of whether they were military personnel or civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Might I show the witness Prosecution Exhibit 496, please. Thank you. I would like to ask that we turn to Articles 140 -- I'm sorry, 141 to 144 for our purposes today. In my version, it's page 32. It is on Sanction, I'm informed. Page 52 and it's on Sanction currently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go straight to the crux of the matter. I'm sure the judge knows these articles by heart.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would just like to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And you can answer as briefly as possible, if Article 142 applied to the members of the army of 2 Corps and the crimes that it entails.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't need him to explain to us --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I was thinking a simple yes or no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: As the assistant commander for legal matters, can you also answer in the same fashion as to whether Article 141, war crimes against prisoners, applied to members of --

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, those two articles, I'd like you to tell the Trial Chamber whether they entail a statute of limitation. How many years does one have prior to being able to cease any investigation or Prosecution concerning those crimes?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: There is no statute of limitations, as a legal institute, because in Article 100 of the same law, as far as I can recall, this Article provides that criminal prosecution shall have no statute of limitations for genocide, war crimes against civilians, wounded persons, prisoners of war and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's on page 37 of the English copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We might remove P496 from the witness at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Judge Hogic, in your capacity as the assistant commander --

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the first time I gave my details two years ago, I have ceased to be a judge. I am no longer a judge. For two years I have not been a judge. I am now an attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You're probably earning more money.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Not as much as the judges and lawyers here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hogic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Hogic my question was going to be in your capacity as assistant commander for legal matters, did you have on several occasions the chance to look at orders or written reports that encouraged and insisted that members conform to the international law and those specific articles of the Criminal Code of the former Yugoslavia as incorporated into Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of the 2nd Corps, or -- rather, none of the three commanders ever issued an order that might encourage the commission of war crimes. On the contrary, whenever there was an occasion to do so, they pointed out the obligation to comply with international law and legal provisions, and they insisted especially on a positive attitude toward wounded and imprisoned enemy soldiers. And I think that this characterised the behaviour of the 2nd Corps from the first conflict that broke out in Tuzla on the 15th of May 1992, when there was a four-day conflict in the centre of town with the JNA and about 200 JNA members surrendered. There was no insistence on a one-on-one exchange or anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like the witness to see now Prosecution Exhibit 29, please. I would ask Mr. Hogic to look at this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Please tell the Trial Chamber: Do you recognise the name of the person who signed this order?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's the commander of the district staff of the Territorial Defence in Tuzla at the time, Mr. Zeljko Knez, and as far as I can recall, this is his signature. There are some other characteristics of this document which might appear a bit odd. In the heading, it mentions the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It had already changed its name, but evidently they used the seal they had available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Can we have the screen split -- on one side we get the English version, on the other side the original one, please? If it's too much work, let's forget it. Let's move because --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It's there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate your efforts, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: As relates to the contents of this document, Mr. Hogic, would you say that this document conforms to what was the general or the applicable instructions that were given to members of 2 Corps during the time period in which you worked as assistant commander for legal matters?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. But this order was issued on the 28th of May 1992, before I arrived in the district staff, and later on in the command of the 2nd Corps. However, regardless of this, this kind of document, which was signed by the then commander, Knez, is something I would always advise my commander to issue, and I would always be happy to sign it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So this -- the principal set forth in this document in its contents, that was never revoked to your knowledge during the time period of your tenure?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We can remove the document from the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, I would like to ask you that in the event of an infraction, a commission of a crime based upon the rules or the laws or the international conventions that you've just described to us, how would information -- what would be the system that information could reach the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply this. This witness obviously isn't testifying as a expert so if he's going to be giving any evidence about information reaching corps commanders, it needs to be absolutely clear that he's speaking of the 2nd Corps in Tuzla and his information, his personal information about particular events and how information on occasion reached the corps commander. We needn't necessarily go into each specific example that that happened, but my learned friend's question might suggest that he's going to give a general expert opinion about chain of commands and how these things happened. Obviously he's not here to give that evidence. He's an eyewitness, he's an ordinary witness testifying about the 2nd Corps in Tuzla, and if the questions could be restricted to the 2nd Corps in Tuzla and his personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't restrict the questions to what happened in Tuzla or in regard to the 2nd Corps, unless we get a clear indication from the witness himself that he's not in a position to answer any other questions relating to any other corps or to the BiH army in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When he's asked questions in this general, way he's going to answer based on his experience in the 2nd Corps and we are going to give evidence being given which is exceeding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. It's a very valid point you raised and the witness I'm sure has understood it. He needs to be very categoric and very precise in your answers. When you are limiting yourself to your experience in the -- as regards the 2nd Corps, then you need to tell us. If you are going beyond, if you know more about the rest of the setup, then you need to tell us as well. In other words, you need to make it clear. Where you don't know, as an ex-judge and as a current attorney, you know pretty much well -- pretty well that we don't need any speculation. We just need to hear from your mouth your own personal knowledge of how the system worked. You can also, within our system, answer and give information that you may have learned from others. That, in other words, you don't really know firsthand yourself but that you have come to know through what others have told you. That is perfectly acceptable in our system. Yes. I think you need to repeat the question, Ms. Sellers. I apologise to you too but I think the point raised by Mr. Jones was a very valid one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, and I think the witness wanted to add something on that subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honours, my experience relates to the 2nd Corps. I will always speak about what went on in the 2nd Corps of which I was a member. Of course, I cannot speak of matters where I was not present, and units where I was not present. As for the Prosecutor's question as to how the commander received information about certain facts pertaining to the commission of crimes or other offences and breaches in the zone of the 2nd Corps, there were in fact two systems of passing on information. One was the so-called command system, where the commanders of subordinate units reported to their superior commander and included in their reports the situation of the unit they were in command of. The second system that existed and that had to do with information about crimes or breaches of military discipline ran through the organs of military security. From the time the corps was established as a military formation, which was in September 1992, from battalion level upwards - battalion, brigade, operative group, division and of course at the level of the 2nd Corps - there were security organs, and these security organs were subordinated to the commander of the unit in which they operated. And they reported to their commander on a regular basis about every criminal offence or breach of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. discipline. The commander of the unit carried out an analysis of these events and he could report on this to his superior commander, the battalion commander would report to the brigade commander, and so on. If the commander did not receive the information, or if he received information from his security officer but he felt that it was irrelevant or unimportant, in that case the security officer had a special channel through which he would report to his superior security officer, who would then act in the same way until this information ultimately reached the military security service in the command of the 2nd Corps. The commander would in this way receive full information about the unit in which a crime or a violation of discipline was committed, and then, in accordance with the results of his consultation with his assistants for military security and in certain cases with me, he would decide what measures were to be taken with respect to the perpetrators. Either a military disciplinary proceeding against the commander or his criminal prosecution by the military Prosecutor. If such was the case, if this was required. In this way, there were two lines of information: one through the regular chain of command, and the other through the organs of military discipline and their chain. Of course, there was always a third, independent source. If a piece of information was not available to the military security organs, or in general to the military authorities and the military units, such information, if it was -- could be passed on in other ways, through private channels and so on. But this happened very rarely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that comprehensive answer. And at the same time taking up from where Mr. Jones had left it, now that you have a confirmation from the witness himself that he's not in a position to speak on what happened out of the 2nd Corps, you should try to avoid asking him questions which go beyond what he has told us to be his limited knowledge. Unless -- if you want to pursue questions relating to other units or other, then you need to ask him first whether he's in a position to give us that information. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hogic, do you know, were you in a position to know, whether other corps within the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina during that time period used a similar system? In other words, was this a normal practice, a reporting system up to their corps commanders?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: I think that was the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you on what my opinion is based. During 1994, in a town called Jablanica and Konjic, we had a consultation of assistants of commanders of all corps for legal affairs, and there we exchanged opinions about the way in which proceedings were carried out in each particular area of responsibility. And from this I learnt that these procedures were carried out in a uniform manner, conditionally speaking. I say uniform conditionally. In all units. I know for example from the presentation made by my colleague from the then 3rd Corps, with its head quarters in Zenica, and my colleague from the 7th corps, which had its headquarters in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Back to -- my question was going to be precisely whether there was any consultation between him and his counterparts in the other corps on such matters. Obviously he has given us an answer. Yes, let's move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, therefore, as part of your function, when information was reported up the chains, whether through either of the systems that you described, would you discuss with your corps commander the nature of that information or complaints or criminal activity?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Of course. The security service, at least when the 2nd Corps was in question, was well organised and well staffed. I think that it comprised three or four lawyers who were very experienced in their job. A large number of the cases that the security service dealt with were conducted in such a way that the service directly reported to the commander and proposed to him a particular measure or proceeding. Only in cases where the commander was not sure that he should accept the suggestion of the military security service, he asked for advice from the sector of legal affairs. Then we would analyse the case together and propose to the commander a certain measure or a certain proceeding to be undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Crimes that were crimes that we just saw under the exhibit related to the property of civilians or mistreatment of prisoners of war, would you be asked your opinion by the corps commanders if that type of information, those types of crimes, reached his office?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: This is a very broad question. I don't know if I'll be able to answer each part of it, but I'll try. We in the 2nd Corps, as far as I am aware, did not have any reports that in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps crimes were committed which would require prosecution under Articles 144 to 145 of the Criminal Code. Probably there were incidents in which, pursuant to an order from the commander to a unit active in a particular area or other units to which this related, we -- he pointed out to them that they were duty-bound to comply with the legal provisions and international conventions. I think that all three of the commanders carrying out these duties in the 2nd Corps paid strict attention to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm moving to a different area that might take a bit more than five minutes. I don't know whether you would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would probably take I would say 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have the break then, but before we do so, Judge Brydensholt has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: You mentioned that you in 1994 had a consultation between the legal services and the people working there. You mentioned also that you don't remember that you in the 2nd Corps had any reports regarding this kind of international criminal-law provisions or crimes. Did you -- do you remember if any of your colleagues from the other corps reported that they have had any of those reports regarding this part of the Criminal Code?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The consultation we had in Jablanica was organised by General Divjak, and it was primarily about issues of military discipline and military courts. I do not recall anyone at that time mentioning anything in connection with the legal provisions pertaining to mistreatment of prisoners of war or wounded people and so on. Our behaviour in the 2nd Corps, in connection with prisoners of war, was quite interesting, and by your leave I would like to explain it further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The way the 2nd Corps treated prisoners of war was interesting. There were rumours that a prisoner of war camp was to be established in Tuzla, as had been done in Keraterm and other places that you are probably familiar with from your experience here. The legal department and my colleagues working with me, we were very much against this. We even consulted some colleagues from the civilian sector. And I think that we acted properly at the time, and that our decision was the correct one, because all these combatants from the opposing army, after they were imprisoned were brought before a court and, based upon a court order, they were put in prison. I think this was interesting from the point of view of the 1st Corps and their prisoners because they asked us about our experiences in this respect and we explained this to them and I think that they received this well and realised that this was the best way to act, not to keep people detained without any legal basis but to make use of the existing legal system, which made mention of actions against the constitutional order of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and to sentence these people and put them in prison. The fact that we later exchanged these men with the aggressor's side - that was the term that was current at the time for the opposing army - we believed that this was a necessary solution with the aim of getting our own imprisoned soldiers out of the enemy's hands, and that was one of the conclusions we reached at this consultation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: You mentioned that you used to bring those prisoners of war before a court. Which type of court? Which kind of judge would that be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, would it be a civilian or military court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you look at the law that was valid at the time, in the initial phase of the war in 1992, we only had civilian courts. It was only later on, as of September 1992, that we had district military courts. These were courts of first instance for acts against the army and army property - I'm referring to the BH army - and these courts then dealt with such matters. The district military courts existed until 1996, when their work was taken over by the regular courts. These courts were established by law and they operated completely separately from the military units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just coming back to this meeting in 1994, I think there must have been a reason to come together, and since you told us that there have not been crimes of taking prisoners and so on which have been in issue, what other points or issues or questions did you have? Or what type of crimes or violations of the law have been the reason to have this exchange of experience in 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, back in 1994, the army had already been consolidated. At the time, a blockade was lifted that had been imposed by Croatia against Bosnia-Herzegovina. Strong links were forged between units. It was only logical that there was a need to exchange our experiences in the number of different sectors. I'm not sure when exactly, but I know that other sectors held consultations too, intelligence, security, logistics, any number of different sectors. I can't tell you more about that, but I know that consultations took place at the time. On the other hand, at this particular conference, it was necessary to exchange our respective experiences with regard to military discipline and the relevant measures, including the responsibility of certain military commanders of the BH army. I'm not talking about the commission of crimes, I'm talking about disciplinary steps to be taken over infractions committed by BH commanders in the line of duty. This was necessary in order to make the system better operational and more effective. An example needed to be set on how a commander should not act, and a new example needed to be set on how a commander should act. The need to do that at the time was great, for the simple reason that the level of training and education of our commanders was on the whole relatively low, especially the lower-ranking officers such as platoon level officers and company level officers. We had very few active duty officers or reserve officers that had come from the former army. It was necessary to take a great many things and to apply them in a uniform manner. I think this was one of the principal purposes and the reason why these consultations were held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Eser. I thank you, Mr. Hogic. We will have a 25-minute break. We will resume at quarter past 4. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, you testified about the reporting system that could come up either through the command structure or the security officers. I'd now like to ask you: What would the commander of 2 Corps do with information, in terms of the possibility of referring it to judicial organs? What could, I'm sorry. What could the commander of 2 Corps do?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: I understand. This depends on the kind of information that's obtained. It depends on whether there is an infraction or a crime, at least in terms of what the information indicates. The commander could take two different courses of action. If there is an infraction of military discipline by one of the commanders of the 2nd Corps, then he initiates the so-called military discipline procedure before a -- before the military court of the 2nd Corps. He would then inform the military prosecutor in charge of discipline-related matters. The Prosecutor would receive certain documents indicating the relevant facts and the type of infraction that was committed, and then this Prosecutor would bring an indictment. On the other hand, if a crime has been committed, a crime of any kind committed by a military person, then the military security department would inform the military prosecutor, the district military prosecutor and the district military prosecutor would then inform the relevant district military court, the investigating magistrate, who would then take the necessary steps, launch an investigation, and according to the system that was in place at the time, the magistrate would ascertain whether there were any grounds for initiating criminal proceedings. Following this, there would be an indictment, the case would be tried and a sentence would be reached. Therefore, the commander could do two things. The first was to inform the m relevant military court in charge of breaches of discipline, for a disciplinary procedure and then the second thing was to inform the district military prosecutor to have proceedings instigated if a crime was committed. The third option was if the commander believed that there were no elements of crime inherent to whichever act was committed, the whole thing might be dropped and no proceedings at all take place. As far as I know, the corps commander never assumed the responsibility to decide on his own on the merits or criminal elements of any given case. He would always leave this to the military courts. And this applies to both Commander Sadic and Commander Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you testified before the break that there was an independence between the military district court and the commander. Is that what you are now referring to and what -- in what you have just told the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. But there is one thing. The district military court is established by a federal law, and not pursuant to a decision of the corps commander or any other military commander. The district military court was part of the general judiciary, the independent judiciary, that was within the system of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Question just for the sake of clarification. Now, you used the term "commander of the 2nd Corps," and further up you would speak of "one of the commanders of the 2nd Corps." You said if there was an infraction of a military, that has been by one of the commanders of the 2nd Corps. Now, which type of commander did you have in mind in this connection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think you understood me correctly, or perhaps I failed to express myself accurately. I meant the three commanders who held this post at various times. There were never two or three corps commanders at the same time. There was always just one at a time. Each of these successive commanders throughout the period of time that they spent in that position would take these measures. I'm not sure if I'm making myself any clearer now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So perhaps the translation or the transcript is not completely correct because it reads, "If there is an infraction of military discipline by one of the commanders of the 2nd Corps, then he initiates the so-called military discipline procedure before a military court" and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I might be able to assist you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'd like to ask Mr. Hogic: Could you clarify for us, what is the in personum or the personal jurisdiction of the district military court as opposed to what you refer to as a military court, I believe, for infractions? Which people may come before it?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: The military court in charge of military discipline could only have commanding officers of the BH army who committed some infraction of the military discipline. Officers and senior officers of the BH army. Regular soldiers were not brought before this military discipline court. The military discipline court only tried cases where officers were involved and charged with an infraction of military discipline within the BH army. The district military court tried all persons alike, regardless of their rank or position. All persons charged with committing a criminal act. It could have been anyone, a captain, a major, or anyone else. I think what you've referred to, the translation, Your Honour, is not ideal because that was not the idea that I had. I may have misspoken myself, but what I wish to say is as follows: There was always just one corps commander and this corps commander decided on all these things being the most senior officer in the 2nd Corps. But of course, in the time period under consideration between 1992 and 1995, there were three different physical persons discharging that duty. Three different incumbents. So I may have used the same expression to refer to all three of them, and that may have caused the misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: The sentence I was referring to spoke of infraction by one of the commanders of the 2nd Corps. Infractions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that is a mistake. I don't think he was ever actually referring to infractions by the commander himself. I don't think that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you would like to put any further questions, Judge Eser, or if you would like to pursue this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Just one quick question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic would therefore commanders say at a unit level, at a platoon level, at a brigade level, at a battalion level, those commanders could they be subject to the disciplinary court if they committed infractions of rules or regulations of the military code?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a situation where a commander of the recruitment office who had the rank of colonel was tried before a military discipline court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to briefly go through a couple of questions on whatever judicial mechanisms or bodies were available. And in reference to the district military court I would like to ask you what was its role or purpose within the structure or -- of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: I said a while ago that military courts were independent from the BH army. I think this is something that you should bear in mind. The military courts were part of the judiciary of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- not the army, the republic, as a state. They enjoyed absolute independence in relation to the BH army or indeed any other institution, just like any other court. Just like any other court of law. This means that any information from the command of the 2nd Corps would go to the prosecutor, to the district military prosecutor and then pursuant to the regulations then in form -- then in force, they would take any steps necessary to reach a sentence in relation to any persons who committed crimes. The commander would only receive feedback on what the judgement of the Court was, but the commander could in no way affect the work of the court or affect the judgement or bring about an acquittal. This was never an option.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And was the military district court, did they have as part of their jurisdiction criminal acts, criminal acts that could be found within the Criminal Code of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: What types of penalties could they impose if someone, a member of the army, were found guilty of such criminal acts?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: All the penalties prescribed by the Criminal Code, and those penalties alone. There were no other penalties in addition to those prescribed by the Criminal Code. Therefore, one could not speak of any penalties being imposed outside the law. Only those that were actually prescribed under the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you've spoken at another judicial mechanism that looked at infractions of discipline. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what types of infractions it could rule on and what types of penalties it could hand down.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: The military discipline court that was attached to the 2nd Corps of the BH army was not part Bosnia-Herzegovina's judiciary. It was part of the BH army as an internal institution, if I may call it that. It tried officers for breaches of military discipline. You had the first instance and the second instance. The first instance was with the corps command and the second instance was attached to the Main Staff of the BH army. Any appeals to first instance judgements would be submitted to the relevant second-instance military discipline court, and this Court would then pass final decisions that were binding and had to be executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Sellers, before you put your next question because the first five -- four lines of his answer unfortunately the transcript missed certain parts of what he was saying. So let's -- with your help, please, sir, we'll go through it again. You started saying the military disciplinary -- disciplinary court that was attached to the 2nd Corps of the BH army, BiH army, was not part of -- can you continue from there. Was not part of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It wasn't part of the regular judiciary, the system of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. When I say the republic, what I have in mind is the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's my meaning. And I may first say the BH army and then refer to the republic so you may find it salute slightly confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No no no, it's just I want to make the transcript clear. So it was not part of the judicial setup of Bosnia and Herzegovina but it was part of what, and then you said if I may call it that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So because this is what was missed in the transcript, Ms. Sellers. And I looked at Madam Vidovic at the time to see whether she had noticed that but I needed some help there. Let's proceed. The rest of the answer is okay. Your next question, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Within the structure of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was there a third type of court that was available or that was legislated?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. And a law was passed to set up a special military court. That was the term. And this military court was supposed to deal with isolated cases at the brigade level when someone who has been indicted, charged with a crime, was at large and could not be brought in. Was outside the reach of the judicial authorities. This was usually referred to as a court martial. A brigade commander had the authority to set one up. And under the law, it could only pass two kinds of rulings: one, to find the accused guilty and to impose a death penalty; and the other postponing the sentencing to all practical intents until the accused can be tried in a regular procedure. In the time period between 1992 and 1995 or 1996, that is when I was a member of the army, this type of court was never set up within the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps and I'm quite pleased, I must say, because the consequences of that would have been dreadful, regardless of what the case might or might not have been. Secondly, the 2nd Corps never faced this situation, never faced a situation where its brigade level units were separated from the corps command and from the district military court. And the district military court had authority to try all criminal cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to have the witness shown at this point P322.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, I would ask you just to peruse the document and tell the Trial Chamber if you're familiar with the judicial mechanism that it refers to.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This is a binding provision issued to the district military courts. It was published in Bosnia and Herzegovina's Official Gazette number 5, 1992. It's a decree law. The district military court in Tuzla as far as I remember was established in September 1992 and it continued to operate until it was legally abolished.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And is it at that district military court that crimes such as war crimes that we saw under the Criminal Code would have been tried at? Is that -- did that court have jurisdiction over those crimes?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if any such crimes were actually tried but if such crimes were committed, then certainly they were tried or would have been tried.
