utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now ask that that exhibit be removed and that the witness be shown Exhibit 321.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are the rules governing military discipline, right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, is that what you recognise as in the document before you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, are these rules applicable to the disciplinary judicial mechanism that you've just testified about to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is this the judicial mechanism wherein commanders, whether platoons or brigades or battalions would be tried in 2 Corps?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, did this judicial mechanism, the disciplinary court, did that function in 2 Corps during the time period of 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So would it be your testimony that the district military court functioned, the military disciplinary court also functioned but only that the special military court was not functioning between 1992 and 1995 within -- as related to 2 Corps?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now ask the witness to be given Exhibit 323. If you remove that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Trial Chamber if you recognise the document and what it contains.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: This is the decree law on special military courts. It was published in the Official Gazette number 12/92. The Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The number is 12/92. It was pursuant to this decree law that -- or, rather, excuse me, this is the one on special military courts. It was pursuant to this decision that a court was to be established under special conditions but like I said before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would also ask to you turn to its 323 in the English version of this same document, under the heading of "Decree, having the Force of Law in the District Military Prosecutor's Office." The ERN number is 00630022.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does the witness speak English or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, he has the B/C/S in front of him. Just for the information of the anglophones, this is what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Okay. Because the way that turned up in the transcript, it was as if you were referring him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were asking him to turn to the English version of the same document. Okay. I'm happy with the explanation, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would just, Mr. Hogic, draw your attention to the section entitled "Decree, having the Force of Law on the District Military Prosecutor's Office." Are you familiar with this legislation, this enactment, of the judicial court? Now did the district military office have a functioning prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. You couldn't have an operational court without a military prosecutor's office. These are two separate functions in the judiciary. The prosecutor's office is an independent body acting on behalf of the state before a court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And the district military court also had a functioning judiciary which also is a very important part of the judicial process, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: The district military court had no prosecutor's office. The Prosecutor's office existed at the same time as the district military court, and these were two distinct and independent bodies. In the judicial system of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Prosecutor is distinct from the Court. It was at the time and it still is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, I would like this document to be removed from the witness and I would like him now to see P498 and we have provided that in a large chart form. If we could have the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, have you checked with the -- they know exactly what's going to happen? How are we going to go about this, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope this would be brief. I would just like Mr. Hogic to confirm, he may point to the section of the chart that we are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic you testified about the special military court as well as disciplinary court and the district military court. Would you show the Trial Chamber, yes, the special military court. Do you agree with how that diagram illustrates the special military court? Is that in conformity with your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My client can't actually see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have him point to that and we are more than willing to have the exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- I think the room, the courtroom is so small that we just can't have everyone see everything at the same time. What I suggest is this: That the question is put, the witness points to wherever, and that all the time, the camera is focused on the witness and to the place, spot, on the chart that he is pointing to, and then the moment he points to a spot on the chart, that we try and zoom in straight away so that the accused and everyone else can follow. Otherwise, Mr. Jones -- I mean, I'm trying to think of how to change this but I don't think there is any way we can do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. There are logistical difficulties and we will make the best of it, do the best we can. There is another issue of principle which I raised with another witness, which is that we appreciate if my learned friend wouldn't lead whether it comes to this chart by asking leading questions obviously, the questions ask him to confirm pieces of the chart. If he can explain the Court it's one thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I was just trying to expedite a bit of the exercise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, you've testified about the special military court. First, could you please point to the graphic, the design, where there seems to be the name special military court.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: It's this one here, special military court. And this part of the diagram shows the organisation and manner of operation of the special military court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you've had a chance to review that diagram. Have you in reviewing the diagram been able to determine whether it illustrates or not the setup, the procedural setup, of the special military court?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. As provided for in the decree law. The entire diagram from the initiator of the proceedings before the special court, that is the brigade commander, the conduct of the proceedings, the trial, the judgement, the appeal, and the execution. Everything as provided for in the decree law.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now ask you to focus your attention and use the pointer to indicate where it is written, I believe, disciplinary military court.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Disciplinary military court, that's in the upper part of this diagram, and it shows how and in what manner proceedings are conducted against persons who have committed breaches of military discipline. And there is another link between this Court and the district military court. This is separated by this dotted line here because the moment it is learned that a breach of discipline is not just that but is also a crime, at that point the military prosecutor hands over the material to the district prosecutor's office independently of the commander's office of the 2nd Corps. In the third part of the diagram, we see the structure of the district military court and its setup. Also as provided for by the decree law. And it describes the composition of the Court, the investigating judge, the jury. The investigating judge under the law conducts certain inquisitorial procedures and the Prosecutor acting on behalf of the state before the district military court. Above him is a higher court. We did not have appeal courts in the military court system. So it was the Supreme Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina which was a civilian court which was the relevant appeals court. There was no military appeals court at the level of the republic or the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Sellers. I can see from here and also from the parts in the transcript where it was zoomed in, that the chart that you have been pointing to is in English. Do you understand English? Can you read English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I can read, yes, better than speak English. But when looking at this diagram, and two years ago in Sarajevo when I was interviewed by the investigators, and also during the proofing for today's session, I saw this and it was completely clear to me. So I would not show anything different if this were translated into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But have you been given the opportunity to compare that English version of the chart with any similar chart which is in your own language? Or is it the only chart that you have been shown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was the diagram shown to me, in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you yourself provide any diagrams to the Prosecution on which this diagram may be based, or this chart may be based?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that during the investigation phase, we drew some diagrams. I was explaining the organisation of the corps command and if I remember correctly, some two years ago I drew a diagram similar to this one but I did it by hand. It was a rough sketch. I think it was a kind of diagram. I don't know whether it has remained among the documents kept by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were a judge yourself so you will understand me completely. Our responsibility is to make sure that you're making use of that chart knowing exactly what it contains, even though it is in a language which is not your own. In other words, that you're not pointing at what may be -- has been pointed out to you but that you know exactly what is on that chart in all the minute details that it may contain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that much English. As a lawyer I wouldn't dare speak English but I know what military court means and other terms of a similar nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. That will be the end of our use of this Prosecution exhibit. Thank you, Mr. Hogic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, you've testified about the district military court and also the disciplinary court, the military disciplinary court. My question to you is: Can one substitute -- can one bring a case that has jurisdiction under the district military court to the special -- or the disciplinary court, the military disciplinary court?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: No. The military disciplinary court was a court more in name than in reality. It tried misdemeanours. We have to draw a distinction between a misdemeanour and a criminal offence. When I say misdemeanour I actually mean a breach of military discipline. This is a different concept from a crime. The district court was independent, while the military disciplinary court was a part of the army system in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And that was the difference. As for substituting one for the other and whether a military disciplinary -- the military disciplinary court could be a substitute for the district military court, no. That could not happen. Crimes were not tried before the military disciplinary court. They were forwarded to the district military court and it was that court that handed down judgements in such cases. Impermissible behaviour in general could fall within the competence of either one or the other, but one court was part of the army system and the other was part of the judicial system of the state.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, would it be your testimony that in your function as the assistant commander for legal matters, that if a member of the army committed a war crime, that it would not -- that that person would not be able to be just disciplined but that that person would have to go before the district military court?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask some other questions concerning crimes contained in Articles 141 through 147, but more specifically is how you in your function as the assistant commander for legal matters would have to give advice or review criminal activity. I would like to ask you: Was it permissible during the armed conflict to destroy the property of civilians by means of burning?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you want the question to be more precise it certainly can be framed that way. If the question is not understandable to the witness, I certainly hope that he will tell me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but I can anticipate what the objection is. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's simply this: Is the witness now going to give evidence as to what the law of Bosnia and Herzegovina is? We are able to read the law and I certainly don't see how this would assist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I think you need to rephrase the question and put the question in relation to a specific part of the code if necessary, I mean but --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. We would go to, I'm asking Mr. Hogic that when he was the assistant commander for legal affairs and he had to look at the international law, parts of the code such as 144, or 147, 141 -- let me turn to a specific provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. There is just another matter, which is this. Firstly, due to the fact that there was a typo on the Prosecution's exhibit list and this is P496, I believe, we don't have the provisions. If it could at least be on Sanction so we can follow. Secondly, this witness has testified that he didn't actually have complaints coming under these laws, so -- effectively he's being asked to address a hypothetical in this situation, would this be a crime, whereas really he should be restricted to what he in fact dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I said rephrase the question, because I don't agree that such a question would be a hypothetical one or that the answer would be a hypothetical one. It's strictly legal -- legal question and answer. I mean it's a question would be, would this be included under Article whichever of the code. And to be honest with you, I don't think we need the witness to confirm that because we can read the article ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We would know whether it's included or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I was just going to ask whether -- if it was under the code. But my question goes to a bit of a different area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then go to the different area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: What I'm asking in terms of his position, the type of legal advice that he would give in situations that related to crimes under Article 142.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: For example, in terms of the burning of civilian property. Would you in your position have to give advice or information to the corps commanders via the legal service on Article 142 as it pertains to burning?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the hypothetical. Really the question has to be did he give advice about burning civilian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you recall the order issued by Commander Knez which we saw in the first part of this session, it states quite clearly that units are told to pay attention to the rules and customs of war, to not to burn or loot and so on and so forth. As the assistant of the corps commander, had I learnt of such a thing, I would certainly have submitted a formal written report and I would have asked him to carry out the required measures against the perpetrators. That was part of my job, of course, were I to come across such information. Other organs were they to receive such information, whether they were intelligence or security organs, or any other organs in the corps command, they would have been duty-bound to convey this information through the line of communication to the commander of the 2nd Corps and he would know what measures he had to take.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, could you inform the Trial Chamber if the position, the legal position of 2 Corps, particularly you, in your function, was that burning could take place if soldiers were retreating from an area?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: No. The fact of retreat, this is a normal military procedure. However, burning as even if you define it as defence, it's not permitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now ask you: In your position between 1992 and 1995, was it also -- what was the legal -- I'm sorry. What was the legal position of 2 Corps in terms of the burning of civilian houses during military actions?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: I think we can't speak of the standpoint of the 2nd Corps, or the legal position of the 2nd Corps in terms of the burning. That's an absurd proposition. We can speak of burning as collateral damage but there will never be an order saying in this action you're allowed to burn houses or you're not allowed to burn houses. You are not allowed to burn houses in Bosnia and Herzegovina under the rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would this prohibition against burning of houses during armed conflict also cover a situation where combatants and civilians were fleeing their houses and the houses were burned to prevent them from returning to those houses?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: The corps commander never issued such an order, nor would I have ever suggested to him that part of an order, a combat order should contain anything like that. That was against the law. It was illegal. It was against the law of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, let alone international conventions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: From your understanding, particularly informed by your position between 1992, 1995, during the armed conflict, was it legal or illegal to burn houses, but first allowing goods or valuables to be robbed or removed from those houses?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, my learned friend is really taking this way too far. She is essentially now treating this witness firstly as an expert, someone who is giving his opinions as to whether certain situations of armed conflict would or would not be legal. We've moved completely far away from actual advices he gave, which -- of course he can talk about if he gave an advice on these matters, but he's being asked question after question about what's permissible under the laws of armed conflict, essentially, which is firstly for Your Honours and secondly it's something which perhaps an expert could address. The Prosecution has dropped their expert. We'll cross-examine this witness as an expert if we -- if this continues in this vein, and ask him about dozens of different situations where it may or may not be permissible for certain things to happen but that's not what this witness is here to testify about. In my submission it would be inappropriate for him to be -- for him to be questioned in this way. We will have to get into this -- into considerable detail if he's going to speculate and give hypothetical advices about what would or would not be legal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think you will need to rephrase the question or drop it, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, in your position when you were the assistant commander for legal affairs between 1992 and 1995, and your knowledge of the rules and regulations to which the ABH were bound, was it at that time an infraction or not to burn houses but to wait until goods or valuables had been taken or robbed from them first?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It is a factual question that the witness might be able to assist the Trial Chamber with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's exactly the same question and Ms. Sellers is supposed to rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. Jones. You've rephrased it but you've put the same question altogether. Go to looting straightaway and ask him a direct question on what was the position of the 2nd Corps as regards looting. And that's it. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I make one final objection on this subject just because we are all interested in dealing with this testimony as expeditiously as possible. If we are going to get into this we will have to cross-examine as to what if those civilians were starving to death; does that provide a Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't allow you to put that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's a question of law equally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a question of what was -- if they had a position on this matter. Because as I take it, it's that the position was one, and that is even in terms of what is contained in the Knez document, I mean -- in our operations and our dealings with the enemy, we are bounds to -- you are bound to observe the law. And we have enough to know that this is not only international law but also the domestic law that was in force in the territory of ex-Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would be surprised if the 2nd Corps required civilians to starve to death, but we'll come to that in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would really object at this point to Defence counsel putting their argument through prior to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but you're not going to get there in any case, Ms. Sellers. So I would suggest you put -- you rephrase the question along the lines I suggested, whether his corps ever dealt with this matter in theory or in practice, and leave it at that. I mean, it's the ends of the day, he's not going to tell us what the law was. We have to decide it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, what the position of the 2nd Corps was in terms --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please then answer the Trial Chamber's question concerning the position of the 2nd Corps in regards to looting during armed conflict between 1992 and 1995. Of civilian property.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Very simple. The 2nd Corps, through the district military prosecutor's office, prosecuted all the people who were found to have committed looting, burning or other criminal offences. If you check the archives of the district military court in Tuzla, you will see how many people were tried. I don't have -- for such crimes. I don't have the information with me. This is confidential information. But it does exist in the district military court in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that neither the burning of civilian property nor the looting of civilian property was permissible under the rules and regulations of 2 Corps? Just simply yes or no, Mr. Hogic.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Not according to the rules of the 2nd Corps, but according to the laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina, this is impermissible. This applied to the 2nd Corps, the 3rd, the 4th, the 1st, any corps that existed on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words -- let's cut it short on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These actions such as looting, such as burning, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. would have landed the perpetrator before -- we have a problem now. Is it -- are you receiving interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I am now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, these offences or these actions would have been prosecuted basically because they were -- constituted a violation of the written law that was applicable for all the entire Bosnian army. That's the position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the position.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If someone within a unit were advocating that arson or the burning of houses should occur after looting, what would be the steps or the advice that the assistant commander for legal affairs would give to that commander between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, yet again under cover of what advice he would give, my learned friend is seeking to have this witness give his opinion into the legality or otherwise of facts which are in this case. It's completely inappropriate use of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Might I respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It becomes hypothetical, completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I respond. It is not -- it is neither under a guise, it is actually directly asking the position of 2 Corps or the ABiH, what advice would they give to a commander. And I think that he has testified that he, as the assistant commander for legal affairs did give advice for legal matters. This is a legal matter. What advice --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First you ask him whether he ever had to deal with this matter to start with. Because if he never had to deal with this matter or this matter never arose while he was occupying that position, you can't ask him now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I will ask him the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You've heard Your Honour's question. Did you ever have to give advice to commanders who might have been faced with the situation of their members of their units committing crimes such -- what you described as crimes such as burning? In your capacity as assistant commander for legal matters.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was discussed on several occasions, at the staff or rather the commander's collegium at corps level. Always based on a report from the security organ and the commander always, and I must add at my suggestion, as well as at the insistence of the security organ, he always insisted that such acts should be prevented as far as was possible and that perpetrators should be punished. And this was important to maintain military discipline and combat morale, because, in units where there was looting, illegal theft of others' property, combat morale always fell. The unit becomes disobedient and is no longer able to carry out combat tasks. All the commanders, Delic, Knez, Sadic, each of them always pointed this out, and they always said it was the worst thing that could happen to the army, and they always demanded that their subordinate commanders pay special attention to this. To prevent such activities in the first place, and secondly, to punish the perpetrators. And as I have just said, the district court had quite a lot of work to do in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move into a different area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, I would like to ask you, did you know of a person named Ramiz Becirevic?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I met him in mid-April 1994 when with a group of commanding officers he arrived in Tuzla from the occupied - or not occupied, it wasn't occupied yet - but it was separated zone of Srebrenica. He was with Mr. Oric. I think there were about 20 of them in that group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you know what his position was, if any, within the structure of the armed forces, or what job or function he had if he were not in the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't know at first. I think he held one of the responsible positions within the operations group and later in Srebrenica, but I'm not familiar with his personal background or training. I think he was a reserve officer with the former JNA and the rank, forgive me if I'm wrong, but I think the rank was Captain 1st Class or major but I can't be positive. I may be wrong. It's too far back for me to remember. I can't be positive about the rank he held.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Are you familiar, tell the Trial Chamber if you know, with any type of training in international law that reserve officers receive or that they do not receive such training?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Well, if there are no objections, I may as well say something about it as I was trained as a reserve officer myself and I worked as an instructor at the reserve officers' college in Belgrade for a while. I familiarised my colleagues with the provisions of the international law of war. There was usually done as part of a subject called the rules and regulations governing the armed forces of the SFRY. As I was a lawyer who was a member of the reserve communications officers' school, my legal background was used and I was given the job of familiarising my colleagues about these subjects, the general provisions and the conventions governing the conduct of war. This was seen as some sort of a general background that all the officers of the former JNA needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In the training, just to clarify, did that include discussions or information related to the war crimes that you've testified about today, precisely those in Article 141 through 150?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was compulsory. By way of an example, in the former JNA, I was there myself for 11 months in 1979. The Criminal Code of Yugoslavia had just been adopted two years previously. It was considered at the time one of the most advanced criminal codes in Europe. It contained the provisions on genocide, Article 141 and so on and so forth. According to those provisions and according to the curriculum of the college, I was supposed to give a general lecture. Those attending would be informed in a very general way on what the Geneva Conventions meant; what our conventions meant; what our home judiciary was; what were the rules governing the work of the armed forces; how one should deal with certain times of situations; how a commanding officer should deal with certain situations; how you deal with illegal matters; how you deal with an order that just can't be carried out; and so on and so forth. So this was some sort of a general background that all the future commanding officers of the former JNA needed and were expected to have. Needless to say, those of us who were lawyers serving in the JNA, thanks to the fact that we had taken the relevant exams at a law faculty, enjoyed the privilege of special knowledge and had much more information to our name about these matters. I worked with ham radio operators also before the war, and this led me, as someone with a legal background, to go to the communications officers' college and I was one of the 100 or so conscript who is were there. And among all these people, I was the only one with a legal background, so they used this to get me to explain a thing or two about these provisions, regulations and conventions in the former Yugoslavia. A few things were said about the constitution of the former Yugoslavia and a number of other matters that may not be of relevance now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Hogic. I'd like to ask you also, are you familiar with the name Amir Mehmedovic?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was assistant commander for legal matters at OG8 for a while with Mr. Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Whether you state OG 8, is that the operations group 8?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes, Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did Operations Group 8 Srebrenica, did that come under the command of the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you have contact in any form or way with Mr. Amir Mehmedovic in his capacity as the legal officer?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Rather, assistant commander of the operations group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be moving into an area that involves some of the documents that Defence counsel raised earlier and I would just like to know if they have at there point in time no objections that we move into this area or we could do it after the break so that they will be able to have adequate time to read and understand a bit of this testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honours. We would like to is a save time to the extent possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Madam Vidovic. You may proceed. You're still almost 20 minutes away from the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I just want to raise it because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. You did the right thing and I appreciate that you did raise the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me one minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that there are a couple of things within the transcript that we will ask to be corrected. I believe it's at line 13, 17, 29. It's going up, but I hope that it will be the name of Mr. Amir Mehmedovic, in terms of spelling and his correct title.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Leave those until later because usually those are dealt with after this thing. Mehmedovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, did you ever enter into correspondence with Mr. Mehmedovic?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. During my work with the corps, some sort of radio communication was set up with Srebrenica. It was difficult, but we succeeded. We asked for the relevant reports and we tried to use a radio link to pass certain provisions and regulations on to Srebrenica. I tried on several occasions in several different ways to have this forwarded to Srebrenica. We tried to have copies of the official gazette, the physical copies, forwarded to or rather delivered to Srebrenica and Zepa. However that proved impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you tell the Trial Chamber what time period --

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: If I may be allowed to finish. If I may. Physical delivery was only possible by courier but the risk was great that the documents would be lost somewhere along the way and in view of the fact that there were several binders, very heavy ones, that needed to be taken there, it was impossible to do this by messenger. The important thing was to get some salt to Srebrenica. That was far more important than all the documents of this world. On the other hand, whenever we received something in electronic form, any regulations or rules, we would use this system to forward these rules to Srebrenica. They somehow managed to get hold of a laptop and use this to maintain communications with the 2nd Corps. I don't know how they did it but they did. The greatest problem was electricity because there was never any electricity in Srebrenica. There was the technical aspect too. They were short on paper. So even those regulations which were forwarded to them electronically, they had no paper to print them out. I know of stories when they first came to Tuzla, this group of officers, I know that even the Court documents in Srebrenica were used to roll cigarettes. We tried to use our liaison officer for liaising with the United Nations to get some documents to Srebrenica. However, UNHCR, which was in charge of the humanitarian convoys to Srebrenica, categorically refused to carry anything that had to do with organising any authorities or anything to do with any military regulations. They categorically refused the possibility. Therefore it wasn't possible to use that channel of communication. There was some radio communication and we got there information in the second half of 1994 from the assistant commander for legal matters. However, those were reports on the situation in the unit there. What the relationship was between the commanding officers and the soldiers, which disciplinary steps were taken, we put these reports together and sent them on to the corps commander, and then he would be in charge of the final assessment and any final decisions that needed making. The situational reports speak about the situation in OG 8 from the legal point of view. However, when I went through these reports, much later, some of the things struck me as quite illogical and I'm not sure how I would evaluate them now. At any rate, those were the reports that we received from Srebrenica. Of course, we in the 2nd Corps were in a situation to print them out and to leave them in our archive and they have been preserved in the archive of the 2nd Corps. Be that as it may, the laptop that was used in Srebrenica was at one point destroyed or rather seized. It was seized when Srebrenica fell. And we don't know what became of this laptop. It's probably somewhere in the army of the Republika Srpska. I'm not sure if this Tribunal has access to it. What is certain is that this laptop contained everything that ever reached the command of the Srebrenica Operations Group, or later, the 28th division. Forgive me for being perhaps a bit too comprehensive and I'm not sure if I have forgotten anything that you wanted me to elaborate on. Please remind me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you for being thorough. I would just like to have you put some time frames on what you're discussing. The time period in which you were attempting to give material or to have materials reach Srebrenica, that was from what time period until what time period, please?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: You see, we, as the 2nd Corps, always had at our disposal all the regulations of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, from number 1 in 1992 onwards. These provisions would be delivered to Tuzla and copies were made there. Each operations group and brigade that was part of the corps would obtain from the corps commander, from my department, or rather my sector, all the official gazettes containing the provisions and regulations of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as the official gazette of the BH army, which was a separate media. All these regulations were always there ready to be sent on to Srebrenica, one way or the other. However, it was only once that -- once the radio link was established by using this laptop that had been delivered to Srebrenica in some way that I'm not familiar with, that a more normal communication, in a manner of speaking, became possible with Srebrenica, concerning everything, concerning logistics, concerning security, concerning intelligence-related issues, everything. I'm not sure to what extent it was used for other purposes. I know that my assistant for legal matters sent me whatever reports I requested. By the way, I knew Mr. Mehmedovic from before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. If I can just slightly go back to two things that you've raised in your testimony. Could you clarify: At what time, what date, did you start -- were you able to use the computer communication between Srebrenica and your office in Tuzla? If you remember.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, it was from midway through 1994 and onwards until the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, also, was there any means or ways that you could send coded messages or encrypted messages via this computer?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: All communication with Srebrenica had to be coded. It was only the last conversations on the eve of the fall of Srebrenica, perhaps a day or two before the fall, that the messages weren't coded. They were open messages, if you get my meaning. So everything was coded. Under the military rules and regulations governing the work of communications officers, when you had this sort of communication, an open communication was not a possibility. Whenever there was a conversation that might have been eavesdropped on my the enemy, you needed to code. You could only have an open conversation when there was ongoing combat, and as far as I remember, the only situation where we had open communication was just before the fall of Srebrenica and just before there computer was seized.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, in your communication with the assistant commander for legal affairs, Mr. Amir Mehmedovic, was that also encoded when it was sent between the two of you?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Of course. There was an encryption service and their job was to code all these documents about to be sent, and then what was sent eventually was a coded message. You were never allowed to send a message that was not coded under the military rules. The only exception there could be was a combat situation when there was simply no time to code the messages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like Mr. Hogic to be given Prosecution Exhibit -- I'm sorry, it's not a Prosecution Exhibit yet. It has a number right now of DA 177180.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, I would ask to you look at the document before you and tell the Trial Chamber whether you recognise it and whether you remember receiving it.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received it in early June 1994. In this document, Mr. Mehmedovic reports on the disciplinary measures imposed in the area covered by OG 8 in Srebrenica. This is one of the first such reports, as far as I can remember. Once he had received a request to submit this sort of information, he sent this back and this is the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, when one looks at this document, Mr. Hogic, the types of disciplinary measures that appear on the document - advice, caution, reprimand, serious reprimand, military detention, prison up to 60 days - was that in conformity with the rules and regulations that were governing at the time period when you were the assistant commander for legal matters?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Roughly speaking. You can't say that all of this is entirely accurate, but in part it certainly is. A reprimand, military detention, these are some of the measures prescribed, disciplinary measures that can be imposed against soldiers. There was no proper analysis here, nothing that would indicate whether any of the commanding officers were punished. Most of these to the extent that I can see were applied against regular soldiers. If you take anything, any of these, with the exception of military detention, this is something that was applied in the labour law of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and these measures might as well have been adopted from a perfectly common firm or regular company where workers were being punished for something by being reprimanded. Or -- even from the Criminal Code of the former Yugoslavia, you could [as interpreted] have a reprimand as a punishment. So this is a borderline case. This is not quite law. But there was the possibility of imposing military detention and also of imposing sentences of up to 60 days of detention, depending on the situation. But that measure is not reflected in this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now like to draw your attention to the paragraph that reads "Since no special military court has been set up in the zone of responsibility." And would you look at that paragraph and please comment on it.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: You see, if we are speaking about the special military court, it's quite clear we can't be referring to the Court that I pointed out on the map, and I mean the special military court covering the units that surround it. Secondly, we see here that there are reports filed by the public security station, SJB, I suppose that's what the reference is to, against members of the BH army and submitted to the municipal prosecutor. And there is a request being made to open an investigation. I don't think the phrasing is logical. I think it should be phrased differently. A request to open an investigation is something that the prosecutor should be making to the investigating magistrate. So this is not regular, strictly speaking. And then there is talk of an investigation against 11 members of the BH army under Article 42, 147 and 148 of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, grievous bodily harm and aggravated theft. There is grounds to suspect that certain crimes were committed and these crimes are here classified as serious crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour there is one matter with the transcript which might need correcting, if the witness can help. It was page 72, lines 9 to 10. I understood the witness said that under the Criminal Code of the former Yugoslavia, you cannot have a reprimand of the punishment. It seems that's worth correcting, if that is indeed an error. Perhaps the witness can help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we have in the transcript is that you could have reprimand as a punishment. Did you say you could have reprimand as a punishment or that you couldn't have a reprimand as a punishment under the law applicable then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, you could have a reprimand being imposed under the former Criminal Code, if I'm not mistaken. Reprimand as the mildest form of punishment. But you must know that criminal law was never my specialty. Therefore I can't be certain about it. I would need to go back to the law to be sure whether there was something that was possible or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I thank you. And I also thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if you would like to take a break at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then question from Judge Eser and then we have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Before we leave this document, the article speaks of crimes under Article 148 of the Criminal Code, grievous bodily harm and aggravated theft. Now, to your knowledge, have these been crimes between soldiers or crimes, violations, committed by soldiers with regard to other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on this document, I really can't say, but it was only after certain people came back from the Srebrenica area in 1995 that we found out that both kinds of criminal offences had been committed. Both amongst soldiers and -- between soldiers on the one hand and civilians on the other. It was sometimes the case that both kinds of incidents occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- yes, we need to decide what you're going to do with this document. It seems to be a defence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No it's not a Defence exhibit. It's one of the documents that came from the collection -- collection. I'm not finished with the document yet so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll deal with it later then. Okay. We'll have a 25-minute break which means we'll start at quarter past 6. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We are still with the document. That's DA --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, does the witness have the document? Yeah, okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, I would like to draw your attention to the last paragraph on this document, and in the English version it states that "with the exception of responsible individuals who damaged the reputation of the RBH army, discipline and soldierly [sic] behaviour of the 8th OG group is rising constantly on a daily basis." Is this in conformity with what you testified earlier about undisciplined troops were bad for morale and for the reputation of the army?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether this has been interpreted properly when you mentioned this last paragraph, because here in Bosnian it says "with the exception of irresponsible individuals," those who are sullying the respectability and the good name of the army. This means that discipline -- is -- soldierly behaviour. This refers to soldierly behaviour. That's how I understand this sentence. If you were referring to something I said before, would you please remind me what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Pardon me. I'm referring to a statement you testified about earlier, saying that undisciplined troops, troops that or army members that were undisciplined were bad for morale and detrimental to the armed forces. And I'm asking whether that last paragraph reflects a bit of what you testified earlier.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you that in your capacity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait. What's that's correct? Because it's not clear in my mind whether that's is what you just suggested to him or whether he's answering your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? May I clarify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unseemly behaviour, breaches of discipline, in any case, brings down the morale and combat discipline of any unit, and what I said previously refers to this. Such behaviour causes a deterioration in the combat morale and discipline of units. So the more such individuals or eliminated from the units or disciplined the better for the chance for the unit to have good combat morale and to carry out any combat task better. A unit -- it's clear to you now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So basically the question that was put to you, whether this last paragraph in that document falls within the context of what you had just been explaining. This is how you understood it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I'm not completely clear. I mean, the last paragraph reads: "Discipline and soldierly behaviour of the 8th OG is rising constantly, on a daily basis." This sentence seems to imply that the discipline had been less good before; that it is becoming better now, but it has been less good before. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: At there point I would like to ask for a P number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. There will become Prosecution Exhibit P?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 538, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 538. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If I may with the Court's permission, at this point in time - I wanted to raise it earlier - I'd like to hand up the ERN number copies of P496, and that's the Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What's the problem with that? You said you didn't have it available but I'm sure you do have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. No, what I meant was we were given the list and so we obviously brought the exhibits that were on the list. Because of the typo P495 should have been P496 we didn't have a physical copy with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We regret that the typo that was corrected last night was not sufficiently understood because there was also a typo that we ourselves had to look at and say referred to another exhibit. But right now we would like to hand up an ERN copy of the exhibit so we will have more facility of going to the different pages by ERN numbers. I believe the Defence already received a copy. We handed it up earlier. And right now we would like to land it up to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this going to substitute the existing 496?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would like to replace it because existing P496 does not have ERN numbers on the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You are correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We remain with the same number or do we get another designation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. It will -- let's, well, let's play it safe here. Mr. Jones or Madam Vidovic, sorry, I mean, it's -- I don't think the question arises as regards the Serbo-Croat version but as regards the English translation, do you have any objection at all if we just replace the previous copy that we had with this?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Please, will you tell my secretary. Otherwise I would need to make a note on it. So this will be the new P496 and it will replace the current one. Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to have another document placed in front of Mr. Hogic and that document has ERN number 04119054.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you briefly scan the document. Does this document reflect the communications between you and Mr. Mehmedovic during 1994? I believe it's October of 1994.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a report I received from Mr. Mehmedovic on the 5th of October 1994, and it's addressed to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, I would like to draw your attention just briefly to the first paragraph. Does that indicate there is a continuing disciplining of certain members of the armed forces who are part of the 8th Operational Group in Srebrenica during the time period indicated as September?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: According to this report, yes. But these are measures handed down by commanders to their soldiers under the rules on military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And among the disciplinary measures that are handed down, would you agree that some have been cautioned, others reprimand and detention up to 30 days?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Up to 30 days, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now I'd like to draw your attention to the next paragraph where it talks about proceedings against more than 50 members who have attempted to cross to Kladanj. What type of infraction, if any, is this, Mr. Hogic?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Probably abandoning their position and going to another area without their commander's approval.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, when you received this report, or the previous report that we have seen in your capacity as your responsibility as assistant commander for legal matters, what would you do with the information?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 2nd Corps was informed of this. However, the logical question arises as to what he could have done at this distance. Tuzla-Srebrenica, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, was this information conveyed by the computer that you testified about before?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you what I did about this report. I informed the corps commander. The corps commander was informed of this immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: My question is was this document or this information in the document, was this conveyed to you by computer, the computer that you testified about earlier that established a communications between Srebrenica and Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Precisely so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did that account for the reason that there is no signature on this document and there wasn't a signature on the previous document?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to draw your attention just to the last paragraph on this document and to see if you have any comment on that for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: The fact that there is no signature is logical because this telegram arrived through a radio communication and it was impossible to transmit a signature. You could just print out the name of the person sending it. This was done through a communication system I described to you previously as only the name of Mr. Amir Mehmedovic is mentioned. We don't see his signature. You were asking me about the last paragraph where it says that they have submitted the proposal of the commanding officers for the establishment of the special military courts as well as the information that they are not in possession of the decree law, and we sent them the names of the commanding officers who could establish a special department of the military court. The law did not provide for the setting up of a special department of the court, but we asked for the opinion of the BH General Staff and we were told that we could establish this special department in view of the conditions prevailing in Srebrenica. And Zepa likewise. So that we responded by the same method and gave them instructions, telling them about the work of the military disciplinary court in the corps and telling them what action they should take and what they should do in order to establish a military disciplinary court in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: This document, I'd like to ask to have a P number given, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this will be become P539; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now ask that Mr. Hogic be given the following document. It's DA 177853.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, I would just ask you to first glance over the document and would you confirm for the Trial Chamber that this was a document that you received from Mr. Mehmedovic.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And without belabouring the point, it was transmitted in a similar manner than the other documents that we have just reviewed, transmitted to you in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, in this report, in the first paragraph, it states that there were no collective refusal to obey orders. Is that evidence of military discipline or increasing military discipline?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: In any case, it refers to increasing military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the second segment, particularly under number 1 and 2, is it correct -- was it correct that discipline could be meted out to troops as well as to officers during this time period?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Looking at the number of warnings or military detentions, this is more favourable than the previous report, and even the two reprimands for officers simply shows that attention had been drawn to proper and seemly behaviour, and this is the assessment of an organ which was part of the 8th Operative Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, the next-to-the-last paragraph refers to a department of the district military court seated in Srebrenica was set up. Would you please comment on that for the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: First of all, a department of the court could not have been established under a decision of the government. Possibly by a decision of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina acting on behalf of the assembly as a legislative organ. A court cannot be established by a government decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Lastly -- pardon me.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, it says here that the command of the 8th Operative Group at the request of the civilian authorities sent a list of ten members as proposed judge-jurors, and this is something I cannot understand. When this telegram arrived from Srebrenica, we commented on this, and we said it was illogical and ran counter to the legislation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As far as I know, this alleged department of the district court never actually materialised in Srebrenica. Neither the Court nor the Prosecutor's office ever came to life.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And was it also during this time period, I refer you to the last paragraph, that gazettes or rules and regulations were trying, at least on the part of your office, were trying to be sent to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: We were constantly trying to find methods of delivering these, and I have explained how we did that. We tried physically; we were not successful. We managed to transmit part of these regulations through the radio, through digital means. How far this was successful I don't know. I don't believe that these digitally transmitted regulations were able to be analysed. They probably remained in the computer's memory. They were not printed out and hard copies were not sent out to the units. I think that's how it was. I think that even in our report, which we sent to them, we told them that we would try in every way possible to deliver this to them but I don't think we -- or rather I'm not sure we ever managed to complete this task. I don't think we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were you ever asked via this communication then to send within your correspondence any specific regulations in their most minimum form or any parts of the Geneva Conventions or any parts of the disciplinary code?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: I don't think we had the Geneva Conventions in a digital format, but we had some of the regulations that we did pass along. I'm certain that those regulations were available in Srebrenica. For example, if we are talking about the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia that was adopted by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We are talking about the republican Criminal Code, it certainly was available in a written form in Srebrenica. It had been used by the regular court in Srebrenica for a great many years. Therefore, all these regulations were available in Srebrenica. On the other hand, regulations of a military nature, which referred to disciplinary courts and military courts, it was up to us. We were trying to deliver these to the command of the operations group in Srebrenica. I'm fairly certain that we did eventually. Whether they reached Srebrenica is not something that I can say.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. The witness never at any point said that he actually knew that anyone in Srebrenica had been familiar with anything to do with the Geneva Conventions. Therefore, I don't think the witness should be asked whether anyone from Srebrenica asked for the Geneva Conventions to be sent over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perfectly legitimate question. The two are unrelated, whether one asked or anyone asked or whether anyone was familiar with the Geneva Conventions are unrelated. So anyway, let's move. Let's proceed. Try to finish, to conclude, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to ask for a P number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. This will be 540.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now like the document DA 170465 to be handed to Mr. Hogic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I ask you to look over the document and to just confirm for the Trial Chamber this is a continuation of the communication that you had with Srebrenica. This is in April 1995.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. But this one was signed by Mr. Abdulah Majstorovic who was the acting assistant commander for legal matters at the time, I suppose. He's another person I met upon his arrival in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So would this be, to your knowledge, the second legal officer or assistant commander for legal affairs that was present in Srebrenica during the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know Mr. Mehmedovic. This is several months before the fall of Srebrenica, but we see that Mr. Abdulah Majstorovic was appointed probably by a decision of the commander of the 28th division.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this be a P number. I want to move on rather rapidly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will become P541.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now ask that Mr. Hogic be given document DA 174343, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, if you could just briefly glance at this document also and confirm to the Trial Chamber that it also is a continuation of your communication with Srebrenica in 1995. It's dated May 1995.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to clear this up, I see that now Mr. Majstorovic is Avdo and not Abdulah. Is there a difference or is it the same person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's the same person. We use the abbreviated form very frequently where I come from. Abdulah and Avdo is the same name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to hear from you. I knew it but I needed --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- I needed you to confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic, would you agree looking at the contends of this letter that disciplinary measures are -- appear to be increasing, that there is less -- there is no refusal for -- to obey orders and it appears to be within the rank that is the attitude towards members is becoming in line with the regulations or rules of the ABiH army?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: That's what paragraph 3 indicates. Paragraph 4 says that regulations should be delivered by communications equipment to the 28th Division, and underneath you see what specific regulations they are requesting. As far as I can remember, we did try to deliver these but obviously because of the size of the file or because of some other problems, they never received the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Toward the end of the second paragraph, I bring your attention to where it says, "Because of the blockades of the Srebrenica territory we have so far received the rules on military discipline, the decree law on the army of the RBH and the decree law on military service which have gone -- undergone amendments." Did that lead you to believe that they did have some of the laws but not the latest version of those laws or decrees?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: I think these are mere assumptions as far as amendments to the law are concerned. These are assumptions made by the -- whoever signed the document. I don't think this was the real situation. The law could have been applied, those three laws that they had received, with no difficulty at all. Now, if there were further amendments that were never forwarded to them, in a legal sense that would represent a drawback but certainly no hindrance to act on it. That's provided they didn't know about the specific amendments.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just ask one other question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: This document, Mr. Hogic, I'd like to refer you to the heading where it says, "Confidential number 060595." Could you tell the Trial Chamber why that -- why that is a confidential number.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Every military report is confidential. On the right-hand side you see that this is matter concerning the Defence of the Republic, that the document is a military secret and is therefore classified. If you have something like this on a document, that is being sent, then when the document is given a name in the files of a certain unit, they need put the number 06 there. This is probably a number that refers to the department for legal matters with the 28th Division. 05 should be the ordinal number. I think this is probably report number 9 from the year 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour I'd ask for a P number for this document also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There will become P542, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to move to another area of my direct examination, and Your Honours, I would like to tell you in advance that I will try and cover one segments of this area within the remaining five minutes and then ask for my 15 minutes or part thereof in tomorrow's session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would that leave you enough time, Ms. Vidovic, to finish your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really need at least three hours, and this 15-minute period usually ends up being more like 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There time I'm definitely not prepared to curtail my cross-examination at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, 15 minutes. And that will be 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour I'll certainly try to keep it within the 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's finish within five minutes' time, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Hogic could you tell as briefly as possible whether the military police were part of the configuration, the structure of the 2 Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Of course. Every unit had a military police presence in it, from battalion level up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, were the military police subordinated in a chain of command to the commanders with whom they worked, whether at the battalion level or the other levels that you've referred to -- inferred?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Within the structure of the 2nd Corps, and that's as much as I can talk about, every military police unit was subordinate to the commander of whichever unit they were attached to. If it was a detachment -- a military police detachment in a battalion, they would be subordinated to the battalion commander. If this was a brigade, then it would be a military police platoon and it would be subordinated to the brigade commander. In an operations group, you had a military police company and it was subordinated to the operations group commander, or later the division commander. At corps level there it was a military police battalion that was subordinated directly to the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: What were the functions, duties or responsibilities of the military police within the 2nd corps?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: The duties and responsibilities of the military police were about organising and securing the rear of the units in the area of the 2nd Corps and all the usual military police tasks, bringing in perpetrators, people who committed crimes. To a certain degree you could compare them to a civilian police. The same way that a civilian police force does for civilians, the military police did in relation to military personnel. They made sure that the conditions were in place at the rear for life to go on in these units. A military police unit should never go into combat. It should always stay at the back, secure all the roads, secure all that there was access to wherever the units were stationed, secure the transport and the supplies, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were the military police in 2 Corps also charged with or had the responsibilities of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HOGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The military police secured them in detention. They would take them to be exchanged. But the actual exchange was done by a special commission and not by the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll stop at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Hogic. We'll give you a rest. Not a long one, because you will be back here tomorrow morning at 9.00 when hopefully we will start and finish. I thank you. You will now be escorted and taken back to your hotel. And we will reconvene tomorrow morning at nine. Okay? The meeting that I suggested we'll have in my Chamber will probably be next week because we have got a few things to -- and I have a status conference as well tomorrow so I will -- I will be quite busy. I will have quite a busy morning. So if we leave it until Tuesday, I think it will be better. In any case, if you have a little bit of time to consult amongst yourself whether you can reduce the time of those two witnesses, the ones I mentioned earlier, when it would be convenient for you to make your submissions on the rule 98 bis because on that then I can tie up with the Prosecution and finalise. All right? And we'll also have an opportunity to discuss a few other matters in camera and then we'll report back to open session later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That suits us fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be resumed on Thursday, 12 May, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
